title: Humanistic AI Conference: Generative Models and the Future of Cultural and Historical Interpretation
location: Gross Hall, Ahmadieh Family Grand Hall, Room 330
description:
Sponsored by the Rhodes Information Initiative, the Humanistic AI conference is designed to foster substantive dialogue between the humanities and the sciences.
The conference will explore questions such as: How might large language models be used to simulate or operationalize historical knowledge? How is generative AI reshaping concepts such as authorship, interpretation, and evidence? And how might current AI models be redesigned to better accommodate humanistic perspectives and theories? 


REGISTRATION: duke.is/HumAIreg


SPEAKERS
(talk descriptions: duke.is/HumAIspeakers)

Lauren F. Klein
On Models and Marbles: Reasoning and interpretation in the Age of AI

Eamon Duede:
This talk examines intellectual distance and impact across the sciences and humanities, and considers how AI may shape the future of humanistic scholarship.

Maria Antoniak

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Applied Thematic Analysis (online)
description:
It’s Monday morning and you open your qualitative research project folder. Thousands of pages of text, distributed across 90 in-depth interviews, await. What’s next? This workshop provides a roadmap for conducting an applied thematic analysis, through all major steps in the analytic process. Participants will learn the benefits of writing a qualitative data analysis plan, to ensure that the data collected are analyzed in a way that best informs the research question(s) and fulfills the study’s objectives.

The instructors will demonstrate how to inductively identify themes, transform those themes into codes, and aggregate codes into an evidence-based codebook that is easy to use and that will inform the study’s research question(s). Some time will be spent on the topic of integrating codes and interpreting thematic structure. Basic data reduction techniques will also be presented Hands-on exercises are included for those who wish to practice the concepts learned.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
location: Witherspoon Student Center, 218
description:
The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. 

The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. Whidbee and Facey will discuss the exhibition during an artist talk event that will be held in the center's art gallery at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 2.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Dr. Dave Fossum | UNC Music Research Forum
location: Person Hall
description:
Dr. Dave Fossum, Arizona State University, National Humanities Center 
“What’s an Arrangement Worth?: Copyright, Folk Music, and the Value of Creativity in Turkey”
Copyright is supposed to reward creators for their creativity. Yet there are no clear criteria for measuring the value of this creativity or how creative a work is. Drawing on a case study from my book, Copyright Consciousness, this talk links implicit criteria of creative value to a larger history of nation-building. The launching point for my inquiry is a policy of Turkey’s copyright collecting societies, who long offered arrangers of public domain folk music only a (10%) royalty on their arrangements (whereas a 100% royalty is common in most jurisdictions). While some arrangers complained about this policy, my ethnographic data reveal that many musicians found it natural. Through analyses of a range of arrangements of folk tunes and songs, I highlight the forms of creative agency often erased by this widespread tendency to minimize their originality. Several factors might account for this tendency, including industry politics, bureaucratic convenience, and legal doctrine, yet none explains the policy as well as folkloristic ideologies that locate creative agency primarily in a romanticized vision of the nation’s past. The stakes of this finding transcend a normative critique of the policy itself. Rather, my analysis highlights how Turkey’s history of nationalist cultural reformism gets reinscribed into copyright, despite its ostensibly identity-blind framing. This finding in turn illustrates a larger claim at the core of my book: that the construction of copyright legality is an emergent and contingent process shaped by a wide range of actors, from courts to composers.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
location: Welborn Gallery
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

description:

Free and open to all 
Join us for our annual Fall Plant Sale to find new southeastern native plants for your garden! 
We grow the southeastern native wildflowers, grasses, shrubs, trees, vines, ferns, and carnivorous plants for sale right here in our nursery. Proceeds support our research in plant conservation and propagation. 
See a list of plants that will be available at the beginning of the sale  
To get the best pick of the plants, become a member and attend the sale on Friday, September 25! 
MEMBERS’ SALE 
NCBG Foundation Members enjoy a 10% discount on plants and the opportunity to sign up for an early access sale on Friday, September 25. 
WHY NATIVE PLANTS? 
Gardening with native plants restores lost connections between plants and wildlife. And since they’re adapted to the soils, climates, diseases, and predators of our region, native plants may require fewer pesticides and expensive management practices and be more likely to thrive in a garden. Learn more on our Resources for Gardeners page > 
WHY FALL? 
Fall is the best time to plant North Carolina’s wonderful native perennials, shrubs, trees, ferns, and grasses: it gives plant times to establish their root systems prior to the growing season.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage

Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

description:

We will be exploring the process used by skilled enslaved African labor to extract this valuable dye from the indigo plants - and delve into the science behind dye production. Visitors will have a chance to view and work an active fermentation vat, and dyeing demonstrations will occur throughout the course of the program. T-shirts will also be available for purchase for visitors to try their hand at resist dyeing.

This is a partnered program between Brunswick Town/Fort Anderson State Historic Site and the North Carolina Maritime Museum at Southport. In 2026, this event will be held at the North Carolina Maritime Museum at Southport.

This is an America 250 NC event.

Drop in and create on your own terms! Your Open Studio Day Pass gives you access to Fusion Gallery’s shared studio space from 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected day. Come in anytime after 1:00 PM and stay as late as 7:00 PM.

location: Saltire Gallerie
description:
The Saltire Gallerie would like to invite you to attend the one-time only Outlander exhibit featuring skillfully crafted costumes from the hit-show, Outlander! This exhibit takes place during An Evening at the Hogg House, a Scottish cultural event focused on cultural sharing and the celebration of the historic James Hogg House’s 245 years of history. The event will take place at the Hogg House’s very own Saltire Gallerie, located at 209 Burnside Drive, Hillsborough, North Carolina, on Saturday, September 26th. Hours for the event will be from 4:30 pm to 7:30 pm, directly following the Outlandish Hillsborough Scottish Festival. 

 

Saltire Gallerie is proudly in partnership with the Scottish Cultural Organization of the Triangle to produce the An Evening at the Hogg House event. This year’s highlights include Scottish highland dance performances, traditional games, iconic food, serene 19th/20th century Scottish and British fine art, paintings of Outlander scenes, and the Outlander costume exhibit! The exhibit will feature one of the main character’s most recognized dresses, the white dress Claire wore while on her journey through the stones, beginning the romantic tale of two worlds. Also featured in this exhibit are Jamie Fraser’s Continental Soldier costume, worn during the scenes of the Battle of Monmouth during the Revolutionary War, and other costumes from the popular series. In addition, art pieces from Outlander’s production team and local artists will be on display. If you love Outlander, you do not want to miss this

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
location: Welborn Gallery
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Heal Emotional Bad Habits for the Good Life You Prefer
description:
Raleigh & Triangle Activities Meetup Group
Yes, you have a codependent relationship with negativity that results in emotional bad habits that destroy your life. So what? Everyone has that stuff on Earth! This is a very polarized planet, which can inspire tremendously positive personal growth. Or not, if you choose to remain ignorant and follow bad leaders. What you need is learn to recognize and handle you own monster potentials so you can live happy ever after. Or don’t, and remain a wreck. Either way you won’t be lacking for company! If there’s one thing Earth is good at, it’s an abundance of whatever you expect to experience. So rest assured that whichever you favor-- miracles or misery -- the choice is so easy that you didn’t know you were already choosing it.

Join us this Sunday Sep 27, 2026 for a free liberating talk on how to change the habits that are killing you. We’re adults here, right? We can talk about current splitting realities without getting paranoid, dramatic, or defensively denying. Earth is on the brink of death or rebirth because the cycles are coming to a close. That’s just how nature must work, since you are an eternal consciousness. Folks who insist on remaining unconscious will experience an unconscious continuation of life, which means they die and then find out the truth. “Aww shucks, there’s an afterlife after all! I guess I didn’t have to live so fearfully.”

So even if you don’t know how life really works, you might want to consider Pascal’s wager. In the 1600’s French philosopher Blaise Pascal said look, it’s worth it to give God a chance to exist. If you’re atheist and wrong, then by opposing God you may have wrecked your own eternity. But if you’re theist and wrong, then believing in a God that doesn’t exist doesn’t lose much, just some idealism and charitable living. So what kind of gambler are you? Of course, we miss the point if by trying to please God then we join an obnoxious society that encourages toxic addictive behaviors like judgmentalism. Most religions start with someone nice like Jesus who makes great suggestions for better living, then rude people take over to justify their inner monster. As Shakespeare said, “The devil can quote scriptures for his own purposes.”

Fortunately, with Earth 1.0 coming to a close we get plenty of lifestyle examples to draw upon for confident conclusions. Like the Dalai Lama says, “If you can’t help people, at least don’t hurt them.” And yet so many people choose to hurt each other! Why? Some folks like to say that humanity is evil and should be destroyed. Presumably they’ll enjoy their judgmentalism until the Earth dies with them on it. Don’t worry though, you don’t have to join them if you change your own bad habits. Reality is a multiverse with endless parallel Earths that survive and thrive. It’s just how higher dimensions work, with every branching possibility existing before the timeline that your current life story lands you in. The more you examine your habitual lifestyle choices, the more you can change your whole life “just in time”.

The more charitable view of humanity is that everyone is just doing the best they can. Be kind, you don’t know what burdens people carry. Ok, but I say people just do the best they think they can. You can always do better if you think you can, and you can’t do what you think is impossible. This is your power to choose beliefs. Positive beliefs support you in always becoming a better person on your own happy ever after timeline. Negative beliefs make you think you’re always failing, so you struggle, suffer, react badly, and become your own worst enemy. God is the direction of eternal positive life energy. The devil is your inner monster that pushes for the worst habits to wreck your life. Either way you get lots of company, so living in heaven or hell is up to you.

For this meetup, make a list of habits that you think are bad and need to change. Review the list to feel the deeper judgments going on. After all, what matters in life isn’t what you have, it’s how you use it. Positive energy makes you feel positive and hopeful, negative makes you feel negative and hopeless. You’ll see how life really works with your own higher plans to incarnate on Earth for lessons in loving self-creatorship. We’ll review common negative choice patterns in human society, and see how easy habits are to change with self-acceptance for the self-esteem that inherits more divine self-worth. We conclude with a guided meditation to forgive and replace old habits with new joys of working with your higher self and soul family.

Welcome! Our Inner Selves Mastery spiritual support group is free online every Sunday 11am-130pm EDT, with the last 30 minutes for a guided meditation. If you can’t stay you can get the recording. You can signup here for this meeting and visit www.signupISM.com for all events, newsletter, videos, and more.

Best wishes,
Carl Johann Schroeder
Inner Selves Mastery
spiritual teaching and coaching

Author Scott Gibson will visit Mordecai Historic Park to speak about his new book “A False Perspective: The True Story of the Cornstalk Fences in New Orleans.”
The Cornstalk Fences are now monuments in New Orleans, but their fascinating story is directly linked to Raleigh and a local family in antebellum North Carolina. The family chose an instrument that could have generated a timeless legacy, a tool not just a fence, but it is now an epitaph. 
​In his new book, Gibson explores the surprising connection between the Cornstalk Fences in New Orleans and the Mordecai family in Raleigh. He will discuss the book, answer questions, and copies will be available for sale and signings.

title: FRESH 2026 Cultural Leaders Panel
location: Artspace, 201 East Davie Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
Learn about the connection between curators and artists from Artspace's current and former Creative Directors!


What does artistic excellence look like? How do curators make decisions? How can arts organizations best support artists in today’s world?  
This panel discussion brings together three current and former Artspace Creative Directors: Jonh Blanco, Annah Lee, and Lia Newman. 
In connection with FRESH 2026, Artspace’s biennial exhibition of North Carolina artists, the conversation will explore the relationship between curators and artists in today’s contemporary art landscape. 
Participants will learn about how artists are selected and supported by arts institutions, the individual curatorial approaches of each panelist, and the opportunities and challenges of the field. The panel discussion will be followed by an audience Q&A. 
 
About the Panelists 
Jonh Blanco – current Creative Director, Artspace 
Jonh Blanco is the Creative Director at Artspace, where they lead the organization’s curatorial vision for exhibitions, residencies, and artist-centered programs. A Filipinx-American artist, curator, and cultural leader, Jonh’s undisciplined practice engages community, accessibility, care, and collective imagination through performance art, education, and social practice. They earned a BFA from the San Francisco Art Institute and an MFA from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Prior to joining Artspace, Jonh served as Museum Manager at 21c Museum Hotel Durham. Their work is grounded in the belief that artists and cultural organizations can create meaningful spaces for belonging, dialogue, and positive community change. 
 
Annah Lee – Manager, Holly Springs Cultural Center (Artspace Creative Director: 2015–2025) 
Annah Lee has worked in the visual arts field in her hometown of Raleigh, NC for the past 15 years, where she is a member of the City’s Public Art and Design Board. Since 2025, she has worked in the town of Holly Springs as Manager of the Cultural Center. Annah received her Master’s Degree in Art History and completed her PhD coursework at UNC-Chapel Hill. Having forged strong interpersonal relationships with artists, institutions, and community members to ensure programming is relevant to our communities, Lee programs art and artists who respond to current cultural issues. Using art as a lens to explore and understand problems, behaviors, and events we collectively face, while placing a strong emphasis on process and technical mastery, Lee continues to expand access for all to engage with art as a vehicle to appreciate and understand human experience. 
 
Lia Newman – Director/Curator, Davidson College Art Galleries (Artspace Director of Programs + Exhibitions, 2002–2012) 
Lia Rose Newman has been Director/Curator of the Davidson College Art Galleries since January 2013. In her current role, she provides leadership for the advancement of visual art at Davidson College, curating exhibitions and related programming and providing strategic vision to create an inclusive, interdisciplinary center of learning. With specific interests in socially and politically-engaged art practices, Newman’s curatorial projects have explored such topics as HIV, climate catastrophe, and immigration. She earned a BA in Art History and a BFA in General Studio with concentrations in sculpture and photography from Winthrop University, and an MA from Duke University.  
 
About Artspace 
Artspace is a non-profit visual arts center located in Downtown Raleigh. Visit Artspace to explore exhibitions featuring national and community artists, engage with more than 30 artists working in their studios, and enjoy art classes and community events for all ages and abilities. To learn more about Artspace, visit artspacenc.org

title: Bach Cantata Series: Odes & Oratorios
location: Duke Chapel
description:
In this concert, two of J. S. Bach's most intimate solo cantatas-"Ich bin vergnügt mit meinem Glücke," BWV 84, and "Vergnügte Ruh, beliebte Seelenlust," BWV 170-explore themes of contentment, contemplation, and spiritual reflection. Selections from Handel's exquisite Italian chamber duets, later transformed into "Messiah," offer a fascinating glimpse into the composer's creative process and the journey from private music-making to public masterpiece.

Free admission. Paid parking is available at the Bryan Center Parking Garage at 125 Science Dr. with ADA parking in the surface lot at the same address.


Learn more about the composition and history of the music in a pre-concert talk by Chapel Organist Chad Fothergill at 4:00 p.m. in the Divinity School's Goodson Chapel.

Families with young children, and those not able to attend the concert, are invited to drop in on a dress rehearsal on Saturday, September 26, from 1:30 to 4:00 p.m. in Duke Chapel.

Bach's cantatas stand among the great achievements of sacred music, uniting theological depth, dramatic immediacy, and extraordinary musical invention. The 2026-2027 series, "Odes & Oratorios," explores music ranging from intimate devotion to public celebration, from chamber-scale reflection to works of festive grandeur.

UNC Global Affairs celebrates 250 years of American diplomacy, and the fifth anniversary of the Diplomacy Initiative, during Diplomacy Week 2026!

 

This weeklong series of events takes place Monday, Sept. 28 through Friday, Oct. 2, and brings to campus diplomats and members of the national security community to celebrate the history of American diplomacy.

 

UNC Global Affairs is also pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy. The exhibition will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center from Monday to Friday.

 

Schedule of events

 

Diplomacy Week 2026 offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. Explore the events below and join us in celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy!

title: ‘United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today’ ADST Traveling Exhibition
location: FedEx Global Education Center, Florence and James Peacock Atrium
description:
UNC Global Affairs is pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.” 

 

Created with support from the Una Chapman Cox Foundation, the 21-panel exhibition celebrates diplomatic accomplishments and traces diplomacy’s role across America’s 250-year history, from Benjamin Franklin’s mission to Paris during the Revolutionary War, to 21st-century challenges such as transnational terrorism, climate change and global health.

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

Read more about the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training

Founded in 1986, ADST is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, 501(c)3 educational organization that has conducted and posted more than 2,500 transcripts of oral history interviews of former diplomats on its website — the world’s largest diplomatic oral history collection. ADST’s collection is a unique and priceless historical record of post-World War II U.S. diplomacy, praised by scholars, educators and diplomatic practitioners alike. ADST is committed to strengthening public appreciation of diplomacy’s contribution to America’s national interests, and enriching the professional knowledge of diplomatic practitioners.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Bowditch Bottoms Wetland Planting (Burnsville)
description:
Join the North Carolina Wildlife Federation, Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy, and Wildbud Natives for a wetland planting workday at Bowditch Bottoms in Yancey County. Bowditch Bottoms is a 87-acre property that contains important soils, farmland, undeveloped forested and non-forested habitat for wildlife, headwaters to the South Toe River, and intact wetland and riparian corridors. It is visible from the Mount Mitchell Scenic Byway and several higher-elevation vantage points in the Black Mountains and the Highlands of the Roan. 
NCWF, SAHC, conservation professionals alongside volunteers have worked together at Bowditch Bottoms to restore habitat, increase biodiversity, and serve as a model for active stewardship. Together on the property through multiple workdays we have removed Helene debris, controlled non-native invasive plant species, hosted a hands-on forestry workshop with EcoForesters, planted over a thousand livestakes, and engaged the local community with a grassroots conservation project. 
Join us to continue the work! During this workday, we’ll be planting over 2 thousand wetland species including swamp milkweed, pale jewelweed, bushy bluestem, and more. Bring some snacks and we’ll see you there!

title: CEE Seminar - Explaining the Exposome: Accumulation of Novel and Known PFASs in Living Things
location: None
description: The pace of production for new and existing synthetic chemicals is continually increasing, rapidly outpacing our capacity to assess risks of exposure to these substances. Studies of the chemical exposome (chemicals accumulated in the body over a lifetime of exposure) have reported the presence of thousands of synthetic substances in human blood and these exposures likely contribute a significant portion of chronic disease risk in the general population; however, we lack critical information on where these chemicals come from, how they accumulate in the body, and implications for human health. Here I will discuss my research group's work towards answering the question: How does molecular structure impact a chemical's potential to accumulate in the body, and how can we use this knowledge to prioritize chemicals of concern during nontarget analysis (NTA)? I will primarily focus on per/polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) as a representative chemical class. Information gleaned from measuring relative affinities of novel PFASs can be used to interpret results of human biomonitoring through the lens of bioaccumulation potential, offering insights on potential exposure sources and novel PFAS toxicokinetics.

title: Participatory Deportation Defense: Becoming Abogades de Confianza
location: Perkins Library 218
description:
Focusing on the role that deportation defense lawyers play in legitimizing the deportation regime, this talk addresses the responsibilities lawyers have when representing people within an unjust legal system. What does it mean for an immigration lawyer to genuinely earn the trust of undocumented communities and become an abogade de confianza? Borja explores how lawyers can work alongside families, community organizers, and participatory defense campaigns to challenge detention and deportation. So doing, they can help center the leadership of criminalized people by supporting mutual aid efforts, court watch projects, and freedom campaigns. Borja's public talk casts light on what effective immigration advocacy can look like and encourages us to rethink the conventional wisdom that good legal representation alone is enough to produce justice.

Yvette Borja is an Acting Assistant Professor of Lawyering at NYU Law. A previous inaugural Laura E. Gómez Teaching Fellow on Latinx People and the Law at UCLA School of Law, Borja has published articles in the UCLA Chicanx Latinx Law Review and the NYU Journal of lnternational Law and Politics. Borja hosts and produces the Radio Cachimbona podcast, which has over 180,000 total downloads. Apple Podcasts featured Radio Cachimbona for Latinx Heritage Month and Women's History Month.

title: Dr. Hortense Spillers Public Lecture
location: East Duke 209
description:
Join us on Monday, September 28th at 5:00 PM in East Duke 209 for a public lecture by Dr. Hortense Spillers, a black feminist thinker of unparalleled influence and a foundational figure in African American literary and cultural theory. Reception to follow. RSVP required (please click the "More event information" button to access the RSVP form). 

Talk title: Oedipal Deferral: Implications of the Middle Passage

Hortense J. Spillers is Gertrude Conaway Vanderbilt Professor of English, Emerita, at Vanderbilt University. She received her Ph.D. from Brandeis University and has held appointments at Wellesley College, Haverford College, Emory University, and Cornell University. Her visiting positions include Duke University's Program in Literature and the John F. Kennedy Institute for North American Studies at the Free University of Berlin. Spillers' scholarship spans American and African American literature, Black feminist theory, psychoanalysis, and cultural criticism. Her influential essay, "Mama's Baby, Papa's Maybe: An American Grammar Book," is widely cited across disciplines and continues to shape the study of race, gender, and power. She is the author of Black, White, and In Color: Essays on American Literature and Culture and co-editor of Conjuring: Black Women, Fiction, and Literary Tradition. She served as a period editor for The Norton Anthology of African American Literature and edited Comparative American Identities for the English Institute series. She has held fellowships at the National Humanities Center and the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences at Stanford, with additional support from the Rockefeller and Ford Foundations. A member of the boundary 2 editorial collective, she has also served on the Executive Council of the Modern Language Association. Among her many honors are the Callaloo Lifetime Achievement Award, the Nicolás Guillén Lifetime Achievement Award from the Caribbean Philosophical Association, induction into the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2022), and an honorary doctorate from Yale University (2024). She resides in Nashville, Tennessee.

title: M. Gessen: Hope, Hopelessness & Human Rights in a Time of Autocracy
location: Page Auditorium
description:
The Rights and Humanities Annual Series is jointly sponsored by the John Hope Franklin Humanities Institute (FHI) and the Duke Human Rights Center @ FHI and is co-presented this year by the Provost's Initiative on Pluralism, Free Inquiry, and Belonging. We are pleased to welcome M. Gessen as our 2026-2027 guest in this annual series.

One of our most trenchant observers of democracy, M. Gessen is the author of eleven books, including the National Book Award-winning The Future Is History: How Totalitarianism Reclaimed Russia and The Man Without a Face: The Unlikely Rise of Vladimir Putin. A Pulitzer Prize-winning Opinion writer at The New York Times, they have covered political subjects including Russia, L.G.B.T. rights, Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump, and the rise of autocracy among others. Gessen's essential book Surviving Autocracy is a bracing overview of the calamitous trajectory of American democracy under the Trump administration. They are currently at work on a biography of Hannah Arendt. 

Free, registration required. Click "More Event Information" below to get your ticket! 

Copies of Gessen's two most recent books "Surviving Autocracy" and "The Future is History: How Totalitarianism Reclaimed Russia" will be for sale in the lobby following the lecture. The first 200 copies sold will include a book plate signed by Gessen.

title: Swift Night Out (Charlotte)
description:
Join NCWF, Mecklenburg Audubon Society, and NCWF Charlotte Wildlife Stewards Chapter to meet the most spectacular aerial insectivores, Chimney swifts. These birds spend almost their entire lives flying, hunting insects, and even bathing on the wing. Having lost much of their habitat to development, chimney swifts now rely on brick mason chimneys for survival. As the sun goes down and the swifts make their way home for the night, chat with local conservationists about chimney swift biology, behavior, and conservation. Discover their miraculous fall migration and observe swifts up close using scopes and binoculars. The night will culminate with the spectacle that is many hundreds of swifts chattering while swirling into a vortex before dropping into the chimney. Help us count the birds and contribute to their conservation efforts.

title: Ackland Film Forum: "Dog Day Afternoon" (Sidney Lumet, 1975)
location: The Lumina Theater, 620 Market Street, Chapel Hill, 27516, United States
description:
Al Pacino and John Cazale lead one of the defining crime films of the 1970s. What begins as a poorly planned Brooklyn bank robbery soon becomes a public spectacle shaped by television cameras, police theatrics, and an increasingly invested crowd. Made in the aftermath of Watergate, the film finds humor, empathy, and absurdity amid a pervasive atmosphere of social distrust. 
This film will be introduced by Professor Rick Warner, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature, Director of Film Studies. 
It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. 
UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event. 
  
About the Series: 
Join the Ackland Film Forum this fall for Socially Charged Crime Thrillers: Snapshots of Social Anxiety, a series that accompanies the Ackland exhibition Care and Concern: Recent Acquisitions of Modern and Contemporary Art. 
As vehicles of social commentary and stylistic bravura, crime thrillers often register the pressures and contradictions of their historical moment. Across nearly half a century, the films in this series stage encounters with political power, public trust, inequality, and ambition through assassination plots, botched robberies, and media-driven spectacle. 
From the crises of the late 1960s to the intensified media environments of the twenty-first century, these works show how genre cinema can capture social anxiety in real time. Each film stands both as a gripping narrative and as a record of a world under strain, where institutions falter and everyday life becomes fraught with conflict. 
The Ackland Film Forum is co-organized by the Ackland Art Museum and UNC Film Studies, housed in the UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: ‘United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today’ ADST Traveling Exhibition
location: FedEx Global Education Center, Florence and James Peacock Atrium
description:
UNC Global Affairs is pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.” 

 

Created with support from the Una Chapman Cox Foundation, the 21-panel exhibition celebrates diplomatic accomplishments and traces diplomacy’s role across America’s 250-year history, from Benjamin Franklin’s mission to Paris during the Revolutionary War, to 21st-century challenges such as transnational terrorism, climate change and global health.

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

Read more about the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training

Founded in 1986, ADST is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, 501(c)3 educational organization that has conducted and posted more than 2,500 transcripts of oral history interviews of former diplomats on its website — the world’s largest diplomatic oral history collection. ADST’s collection is a unique and priceless historical record of post-World War II U.S. diplomacy, praised by scholars, educators and diplomatic practitioners alike. ADST is committed to strengthening public appreciation of diplomacy’s contribution to America’s national interests, and enriching the professional knowledge of diplomatic practitioners.

 

- - -

Diplomacy Week offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: RISE to the Challenge: Statistical Considerations for Rare Disease Clinical Investigations
location: None
description:
This public workshop, co-convened by Duke Margolis and the FDA Rare Disease Innovation Hub, will explore statistical considerations in the design, conduct, and analysis of clinical investigations for rare disease medical products. The small patient populations inherent to rare disease present unique challenges that increase the risk of obtaining inconclusive trial results. Addressing these challenges requires careful attention to statistical rigor while utilizing tailored approaches that are necessary to make medical product development feasible in this space. Reliable and timely evidence that relies on data from all available information is critically important to patients and families affected by rare diseases, making the optimization of clinical investigation design, conduct, and analysis a matter of both scientific and ethical urgency.

The workshop will focus on key statistical considerations for tailored approaches employed across the full arc of rare disease development programs. Topics will include the role of randomization and blinding, strategies for enhancing efficiency, and factors specific to medical devices. Discussions will explore these statistical considerations with the goal of identifying efficient approaches that maintain scientific rigor and produce meaningful results for rare disease product development.

Statistical considerations affect every aspect of drug development, testing, and review, including clinical trial design and measuring product effectiveness; understanding the role of statistical review is important for sponsors, patients, and disease advocates alike.  All members of the rare disease community, regardless of prior familiarity with statistical approaches, are encouraged to attend.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: The 2026 Emerging Pedagogies Summit
location: JB Duke Hotel
description:
The 2026 Emerging Pedagogies Summit: AI and Teaching Futures is a pedagogy-focused opportunity for Duke faculty and instructors to explore the future of teaching and learning.

The Summit will create space for curiosity, honest dialogue, and practical exploration of AI in teaching and learning. Whether participants are enthusiastic adopters, thoughtful skeptics, or hold divergent opinions of AI, the Summit invites faculty and instructors to engage with new ideas, challenge assumptions, and learn alongside colleagues.

Rather than prescribing or accepting a single vision for the future of education, the Emerging Pedagogies Summit aims to spark conversations that will continue long after the event concludes. Our goal is for every participant to leave inspired and motivated to shape the future of teaching and learning, particularly as that future pertains to AI and pedagogy.

Event Format

The Summit is intentionally designed as a two-part experience. The morning begins with three hands-on workshops, with participants joining a concurrent workshop facilitated by nationally-recognized educators and pedagogy thought leaders. These two-hour workshops give instructors the time and space to dig deeply into ideas, develop new capacities, and engage in meaningful dialogue with colleagues in a smaller setting.

The afternoon brings everyone together for a shared experience that builds on ideas and practices surfaced during the morning sessions. Following lunch and opening remarks, our Community Conversation session will feature Duke students and instructors sharing short presentations and engaging in structured dialogue about AI and education. The Summit's final session will feature moderated reflections about the ideas that surfaced throughout the day and speculations about the futures for teaching and learning we are willing to build.

Following closing remarks, we will end the day together with a happy hour infused with poetry and play. After exploring difficult questions, experimenting with new approaches, and developing new capacities, we'll make space for connection, creativity, and hope as we imagine new possibilities for teaching and learning.

title: Benjamin Franklin and the Invention of American Diplomacy
location: FedEx Global Education Center, DeBerry Board Room (3009)
description:
How did Benjamin Franklin help shape America’s place in the world?

 

Tom Selinger, retired U.S. Foreign Service officer and “Century of Service and Sacrifice” project manager at the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training, will explore the life, legacy and lasting influence of America’s first diplomat. Selinger’s presentation will examine Franklin’s diplomatic achievements and their enduring impact on U.S. foreign relations.

 

Tuesday, Sept. 29

11 a.m. – 12 p.m.

DeBerry Board Room (3009), FedEx Global Education Center

 

This event is open to all UNC-Chapel Hill students and faculty. Registration is strongly encouraged.

 

Learn more about Tom Selinger

Tom Selinger served 27 years in the U.S. Foreign Service with experience ranging from Kyrgyzstan to Denmark and security cooperation to American citizen services. In his retirement, he works for the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training, a nonprofit where he directs outreach efforts to promote public understanding of the work of America’s diplomats. Prior to joining the Foreign Service, he served as an intelligence officer in the U.S. Army and worked as a political specialist for the Canadian government. Selinger received his bachelor’s degree in magazine journalism and foreign languages and linguistics from Drake University. He is married to fellow diplomat Kirsten Selinger and has four children and three grandchildren.

title: Postdoc Research Communication Series: The Art of Research Communication
location: Virtual
description:
WHAT: Postdoc Research Communication Series: The Art of Research Communication
WHEN: Tues Sept 29, Tues Oct 6, and Tues Oct 13, 11 am - 12 pm
REGISTER: https://sites.duke.edu/mentoringandcommunication/

Sure, your research on fill-in-the-blank is fascinating and important, but in order to help the public understand why it matters (and why they should support it!), you need to be able to communicate what you do in ways that are clear and engaging. In this 3-part series, noted Research Communication expert Jory Weintraub PhD will teach you how to communicate your research effectively, no matter what field you are in - Humanities, Social Sciences, or STEM. 

Session 1: Research Communication Fundamentals, Tues Sept 29, 11 am-12 pm
This activity-based session will introduce the fundamentals of research communication.

Session 2: Communicating Your Research Through Storytelling, Tues Oct 6, 11 am-12 pm
Research demonstrates that people learn new information more effectively, understand it better and remember it longer when it is delivered in the form of a story. In this session, we'll dig more deeply into this and discuss the elements of great storytelling.
  
Session 3: Engaging the Public in Your Research Through Outreach, Tues Oct 13, 11 am-12 pm
Once you've learned the fundamentals of research communication and how to tell the story of your work, it's time to apply these skills by engaging the public through outreach. This session will introduce and explore strategies for outreach, and participants will develop their own outreach plan.

Speaker: Jory Weintraub PhD is Director of Science Engagement at NC State University. From 2015-2022 he was Science Communication Director with Duke Science & Society and taught undergraduate and graduate courses in science communication. He received a PhD in Immunology, did a postdoc in STEM education, and has spent the last 25 years doing, teaching and coaching science communication and outreach.

title: The 1868 North Carolina Constitution
location: Wilson Library , Pleasants Assembly Room
description:
North Carolina’s 1868 Constitution rebuilt the state after the Civil War, expanding political participation and redefining the relationship between government and citizens in the state’s first attempt at multiracial democracy. This lecture examines how that document laid the groundwork for principles that continue to shape North Carolina constitutional law, and what its lessons offer for constitutional debates still unresolved 250 years after the state’s founding. 

 

Speakers: Marcus Gadson, associate professor of law, and Harry L. Watson, Atlanta Distinguished Professor of Southern Culture 

 

About the Speakers:

 

Professor Marcus Gadson is an associate professor of law at UNC School of Law, joining the faculty in 2025. He teaches courses on State Constitutional Law, federal Constitutional Law, and civil procedure. He is one of the nation’s leading authorities on state constitutions and has published a book arguing that constitutional crises at the state level have profoundly shaped American constitutional law and co-authored a casebook about state constitutions. Before joining Carolina, Professor Gadson taught at Campbell University School of Law and practiced at Steptoe & Johnson in Washington, D.C. 

 

Professor Harry L. Watson is the Atlanta Distinguished Professor of Southern Culture at UNC-Chapel Hill. A native of Greensboro, he researches the political, social and intellectual history of the antebellum South and Jacksonian America, including the formation of political parties and the relationship between race and class under slavery. He directed the UNC Center for the Study of the American South from 1999 to 2012 and edited its journal, Southern Cultures, from 1993 to 2019. He is the author or editor of eight books, including Liberty and Power: The Politics of Jacksonian America and Building the American Republic, Volume 1: A Narrative History to 1877. Watson holds a bachelor's from Brown University and a doctorate from Northwestern.

title: Diplomacy Week 2026
location: FedEx Global Education Center
description:
UNC Global Affairs celebrates 250 years of American diplomacy, and the fifth anniversary of the Diplomacy Initiative, during Diplomacy Week 2026!

 

This weeklong series of events takes place Monday, Sept. 28 through Friday, Oct. 2, and brings to campus diplomats and members of the national security community to celebrate the history of American diplomacy.

 

UNC Global Affairs is also pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy. The exhibition will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center from Monday to Friday.

 

Schedule of events

 

Diplomacy Week 2026 offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. Explore the events below and join us in celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy!

 

Visit the Diplomacy Week 2026 webpage for a complete list of events.

 

MONDAY, SEPT. 28

Meet-and-greet with fellow U.S. exchange alumni

10 – 11 a.m. 

DeBerry Board Room (3009), FedEx Global Education Center 

The U.S. Exchange Alumni Fellow for the Southeast, UNC Global Affairs, and the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training invite all U.S. Citizen Exchange Alumni in North Carolina to mingle during a brief, informal networking event.

 

The Ambassador and the General: Diplomacy, special operations and ‘the dark arts’

2:30 – 3:30 p.m. 

Fourth Floor, FedEx Global Education Center

Vice Provost for Global Affairs and Chief Global Officer Barbara Stephenson speaks with a high-ranking officer from the U.S. Army. They will discuss how diplomats and special operations work together overseas to advance American interests.

 

Opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 and ADST exhibition

5 – 7 p.m.

Florence and James Peacock Atrium, FedEx Global Education Center

Join UNC Global Affairs in honoring North Carolina’s contributions to American diplomacy. Students, faculty, staff, administrators, alumni and community members are invited to celebrate with food, drinks and conversation. Vice Provost for Global Affairs and Chief Global Officer Barbara Stephenson, U.S. Ambassador (ret.) Robert Pearson and Tom Selinger deliver remarks.

 

ADST exhibition: “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today”

Sept. 28 – Oct. 2

Florence and James Peacock Atrium, FedEx Global Education Center

UNC Global Affairs is also pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.”

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

TUESDAY, SEPT. 29

Benjamin Franklin and the invention of American diplomacy

11 a.m. – 12 p.m.

DeBerry Board Room (3009), FedEx Global Education Center

Tom Selinger, retired U.S. Foreign Service officer and Century of Service project manager at ADST, presents on the life and legacy of Benjamin Franklin as America’s first diplomat. 

 

ADST exhibition: “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today”

Sept. 28 – Oct. 2

Florence and James Peacock Atrium, FedEx Global Education Center

UNC Global Affairs is also pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.”

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

WEDNESDAY, SEPT. 30

The U.S.-Japan Career Landscape: Government, JET, business, and the nonprofit sector

11:15 a.m. – 12:15 p.m. 

DeBerry Board Room (3009), FedEx Global Education Center

Margot Carrington and Michi Calcagno discuss different career paths for Japanese language learners. Students who are studying Japanese language, or are interested in studying Japanese, will learn about career opportunities in the U.S. government, the private sector (not-for-profit and for-profit) and academia. 

 

Inside the Foreign Service: The role of the public affairs officer

1:30 – 2:30 p.m. 

DeBerry Board Room (3009), FedEx Global Education Center

UNC Global Affairs has launched a new series of events called Visiting Diplomats, and this event with Margot Carrington is the first installment. Carrington is a retired U.S. Foreign Service Officer who served as a public affairs officer. She discusses her career track, including her four tours in Japan, with Vice Provost for Global Affairs and Chief Global Officer Barbara Stephenson.

 

ADST exhibition: “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today”

Sept. 28 – Oct. 2

Florence and James Peacock Atrium, FedEx Global Education Center

UNC Global Affairs is also pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.”

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

THURSDAY, OCT. 1

The role of the CIA in U.S. foreign policy

3:30 – 4:30 p.m. 

DeBerry Board Room (3009), FedEx Global Education Center

Vice Provost for Global Affairs and Chief Global Officer Barbara Stephenson discusses the CIA’s role in U.S. foreign policy with a case officer and Carolina alumnus. 

 

‘Never A Bad Peace: Celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy’ with Adam Howard

5:30 – 6:30 p.m.

Nelson Mandela Auditorium, FedEx Global Education Center

In 1783, Benjamin Franklin wrote, “May we never see another War! for in my Opinion there never was a good War, or a bad Peace.” In this Diplomatic Discussion, the keynote lecture of Diplomacy Week 2026, Adam Howard, former chief historian at the U.S. Department of State, discusses three pivotal moments in American history shaped by the work of talented diplomats: the Revolutionary War, the Civil War and the aftermath of World War II. Vice Provost for Global Affairs and Chief Global Officer Barbara Stephenson conducts a fireside chat, followed by questions from students in the audience. Afterwards, join Howard and Stephenson in the Florence and James Peacock Atrium for pizza and discussion.

 

ADST exhibition: “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today”

Sept. 28 – Oct. 2

Florence and James Peacock Atrium, FedEx Global Education Center

UNC Global Affairs is also pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.”

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

FRIDAY, OCT. 2

Crash course on reading memos and cables

11 a.m. – 12 p.m.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: ‘United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today’ ADST Traveling Exhibition
location: FedEx Global Education Center, Florence and James Peacock Atrium
description:
UNC Global Affairs is pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.” 

 

Created with support from the Una Chapman Cox Foundation, the 21-panel exhibition celebrates diplomatic accomplishments and traces diplomacy’s role across America’s 250-year history, from Benjamin Franklin’s mission to Paris during the Revolutionary War, to 21st-century challenges such as transnational terrorism, climate change and global health.

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

Read more about the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training

Founded in 1986, ADST is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, 501(c)3 educational organization that has conducted and posted more than 2,500 transcripts of oral history interviews of former diplomats on its website — the world’s largest diplomatic oral history collection. ADST’s collection is a unique and priceless historical record of post-World War II U.S. diplomacy, praised by scholars, educators and diplomatic practitioners alike. ADST is committed to strengthening public appreciation of diplomacy’s contribution to America’s national interests, and enriching the professional knowledge of diplomatic practitioners.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

Margot Carrington is a retired U.S. Foreign Service Officer who served four tours in Japan, and Michi Calcagno is the executive director of the Japan-America Society of North Carolina.

 

Wednesday, Sept. 30

11:15 a.m. – 12:15 p.m.

DeBerry Board Room (3009), FedEx Global Education Center

 

This event is open to all UNC-Chapel Hill students and faculty. Registration is strongly encouraged.

 

Learn more about Margot Carrington and Michi Calcagno

Margot Carrington is a retired U.S. Foreign Service officer who served with the U.S. Department of State for 25 years. During that time, she served four tours in Japan, most recently from 2014-2018. In that role, Margot oversaw staff throughout the country and served as Ambassador Caroline Kennedy’s advisor on all public diplomacy-related matters. Margot’s achievements and dedication to strengthening U.S.-Japan cultural exchange and supporting women’s empowerment have been recognized with numerous awards. Margot speaks Japanese, Malay, Spanish and French. She graduated from the University of Florida with a bachelor’s degree in political science and a master’s degree in international relations.

 

Michi Calcagno is the executive director of the Japan-America Society of North Carolina, leading statewide programs, community engagement and operational initiatives that advance the organization’s mission to foster cultural, educational and business ties between North Carolina and Japan. Before JASNC, she spent 20 years in California’s telecommunications industry. Michi is a proud member of the U.S.-Japan Council. She earned a bachelor’s degree in economics from Lafayette College and a master of business administration from Cornell University. Her foundation in Japanese language and culture began with a summer program at Middlebury College followed by a year in Tokyo at Sophia University.

title: Mental Health Awareness for Leaders
description:
Managing individuals who may be struggling with stress, anxiety, depression and other mental health concerns can be a difficult balancing act. Your role is to manage performance and to bring out the best in your workforce, but accomplishing this often requires you to express concern and support when employees struggle emotionally. Managers often feel uncomfortable in this aspect of their role and may lack the important skills of “emotional management.” This course covers ways employees may present their distress and offers insights and strategies on forging supportive empathic alliances within the role of manager. The session also identifies common mistakes managers make in responding to employees in distress and explains communication skills that express support and convey positive expectancy. Participants are also given information on how to refer employees to the Employee Assistance Program.

title: Swift Night Out (Charlotte)
description:
Join NCWF, Mecklenburg Audubon Society, and NCWF Charlotte Wildlife Stewards Chapter to meet the most spectacular aerial insectivores, Chimney swifts. These birds spend almost their entire lives flying, hunting insects, and even bathing on the wing. Having lost much of their habitat to development, chimney swifts now rely on brick mason chimneys for survival. As the sun goes down and the swifts make their way home for the night, chat with local conservationists about chimney swift biology, behavior, and conservation. Discover their miraculous fall migration and observe swifts up close using scopes and binoculars. The night will culminate with the spectacle that is many hundreds of swifts chattering while swirling into a vortex before dropping into the chimney. Help us count the birds and contribute to their conservation efforts.

description:
