Join volunteers at Code with the Carolinas for the biweekly meeting about OpenCourts, a project to build an open data portal for North and South Carolina legal data.. Starting with aggregate datasets from South Carolina courts, volunteers will be working to adopt this data (and our site being constructed to host it) to standards and measures more usable for accountability and analysis. These principles of analysis are drawn from guidance provided by the legal accountability organization [Measures for Justice](https://measuresforjustice.org/), whose limited work in the Carolinas we are trying to renew and expand.

This effort is building toward multi-state data portal that catalogues and publishes trusted, permissively-licensed court records to ensure open legal data remains a **public good** accessible to everyone. ️

Anyone welcome whether an already identified volunteer on the project or just curious. We do encourage new participants to fill out this [interest form](https://forms.office.com/pages/responsepage.aspx?id=DQSIkWdsW0yxEjajBLZtrQAAAAAAAAAAAAO__cyETRVUOTZDSDlCQ0cxRThFMEVUUFNRWkZES08zSy4u&route=shorturl).

UNC Global Affairs celebrates 250 years of American diplomacy, and the fifth anniversary of the Diplomacy Initiative, during Diplomacy Week 2026!

UNC Global Affairs is also pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy. The exhibition will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center from Monday to Friday.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: ‘United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today’ ADST Traveling Exhibition
location: FedEx Global Education Center, Florence and James Peacock Atrium
description:
UNC Global Affairs is pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.” 

 

Created with support from the Una Chapman Cox Foundation, the 21-panel exhibition celebrates diplomatic accomplishments and traces diplomacy’s role across America’s 250-year history, from Benjamin Franklin’s mission to Paris during the Revolutionary War, to 21st-century challenges such as transnational terrorism, climate change and global health.

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

Read more about the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training

Founded in 1986, ADST is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, 501(c)3 educational organization that has conducted and posted more than 2,500 transcripts of oral history interviews of former diplomats on its website — the world’s largest diplomatic oral history collection. ADST’s collection is a unique and priceless historical record of post-World War II U.S. diplomacy, praised by scholars, educators and diplomatic practitioners alike. ADST is committed to strengthening public appreciation of diplomacy’s contribution to America’s national interests, and enriching the professional knowledge of diplomatic practitioners.

 

- - - 

This event is a part of Diplomacy Week 2026! Diplomacy Week offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. Explore other events on the UNC Global Affairs website and join us in celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy!

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: ‘Never A Bad Peace: Celebrating 250 Years of American Diplomacy’ with Adam Howard
location: FedEx Global Education Center, Nelson Mandela Auditorium
description:
In 1783, Benjamin Franklin wrote, “May we never see another War! for in my Opinion there never was a good War, or a bad Peace.”

 

In this Diplomatic Discussion, the keynote lecture of Diplomacy Week 2026, Adam Howard, former chief historian at the U.S. Department of State, discusses three pivotal moments in American history shaped by the work of talented diplomats: the Revolutionary War, the Civil War and the aftermath of World War II.

 

Vice Provost for Global Affairs and Chief Global Officer Barbara Stephenson conducts a fireside chat, followed by questions from students in the audience. Afterwards, join Howard and Stephenson in the Florence and James Peacock Atrium for pizza and discussion.

 

Thursday, Oct. 1

5:30 p.m. (doors open at 5 p.m.)

Nelson Mandela Auditorium, FedEx Global Education Center

 

This event is open to the public. Plan to attend? Let us know! CLE credit is available.

 

Learn more about Adam Howard

Adam Howard is the executive director of the International Churchill Society, a nonprofit organization dedicated to preserving the legacy of Winston Churchill and advancing the study of leadership in times of crisis. Previously, he served as the U.S. Department of State’s chief historian where he oversaw publication of the Foreign Relations of the United States series, trained diplomats through applied history programs, and provided historical context to senior policymakers to support more informed decision-making. Howard received a doctoral degree in history from the University of Florida and currently serves as an adjunct professor of history and international affairs at George Washington University.

 

- - -

This event is a part of Diplomacy Week 2026! Diplomacy Week offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. Explore other events on the UNC Global Affairs website and join us in celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy!

title: Oct 1 - APAC AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our APAC time-zone friendly virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Time, Date and Location**

Oct 1, 2026
6:00 PM - 8:00 PM PDT
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/apac-ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-october-1-2026)**

**Beyond Exact Matches: Detecting Modified 3D Assets at Marketplace Scale**

How can a marketplace identify copied 3D assets when their orientation, geometry, or composition has changed? Drawing on my work in 3D content understanding at Roblox, this talk will explore multi-view and rotation-invariant representations for similarity and duplicate detection, including the challenges posed by deformed and fragmented copies.
It will examine how geometric and semantic signals can complement one another, and discuss practical trade-offs in evaluating detection quality and deploying these methods at scale. The presentation will draw on published patent applications and publicly shareable examples to offer practical lessons for engineers building visual search, content-understanding, and marketplace-safety systems.

*About the Speaker*

[Phani Harish Wajjala](https://www.linkedin.com/in/harish-wajjala-81a47119/) is a Principal Machine Learning Engineer at Roblox specializing in 3D computer vision, multimodal AI, and large-scale content understanding.

**Sign Language: Towards Sign Understanding for Robot Autonomy**

Navigational signs are common aids for human wayfinding and scene understanding, but are underutilized by robots. We argue that they benefit robot navigation and scene understanding, by directly encoding privileged information on actions, spatial regions, and relations.

Interpreting signs in open-world settings remains a challenge owing to the complexity of scenes and signs, but recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) make this feasible. To advance progress in this area, we introduce the task of visual sign grounding, which parses locations and associated directions from signs, and maps them to region in the sign’s local environment.

Additionally, we present a baseline approach using VLMs, and demonstrate their promise on the task. We also outline different applications, such as localization and navigation, which benefit from the spatial-symbolic information encoded by navigational signs.

*About the Speaker*

[Nicky Zimmerman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nicky-zimmerman-41b71694/) I am a postdoctoral researcher in NUS, working on open world navigation. My PhD thesis focused on human-inspired strategies for semantic localization and mapping. Previously, I worked as computer vision algorithm developer in General Motors and Intel.

**MeMo: Memory as a Model**

Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across a wide range of tasks, but remain frozen after pretraining until subsequent updates. Many real-world applications require timely, domain-specific information, motivating the need for efficient mechanisms to incorporate new knowledge.

In this paper, we introduce MeMo (Memory as a Model), a modular framework that encodes new knowledge into a dedicated Memory model while keeping the LLM unchanged. Compared to existing methods, MeMo offers several advantages: (a) it captures complex cross-document relationships, (b) it is robust to retrieval noise, (c) it avoids catastrophic forgetting in the LLM, (d) it does not require access to the LLM’s weights or output logits that enabling plug-and-play integration with both open and proprietary LLMs, and (e) its retrieval cost is independent of corpus size at inference time.

Our experiments on three benchmarks, BrowseComp-Plus, NarrativeQA, and MuSiQue, show that MeMo achieves strong performance compared to existing methods across diverse settings.

*About the Speaker*

[Arun Verma](https://www.linkedin.com/in/arunverma100) is a Postdoctoral Associate at the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology Centre, where he works with Daniela Rus, Armando Solar-Lezama, and Bryan Low.

title: Diplomacy Week 2026
location: FedEx Global Education Center
description:
UNC Global Affairs celebrates 250 years of American diplomacy, and the fifth anniversary of the Diplomacy Initiative, during Diplomacy Week 2026!

 

This weeklong series of events takes place Monday, Sept. 28 through Friday, Oct. 2, and brings to campus diplomats and members of the national security community to celebrate the history of American diplomacy.

 

UNC Global Affairs is also pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy. The exhibition will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center from Monday to Friday.

 

Schedule of events

 

Diplomacy Week 2026 offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. Explore the events below and join us in celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. title: ‘United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today’ ADST Traveling Exhibition
location: FedEx Global Education Center, Florence and James Peacock Atrium
description:
UNC Global Affairs is pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.” 

 

Created with support from the Una Chapman Cox Foundation, the 21-panel exhibition celebrates diplomatic accomplishments and traces diplomacy’s role across America’s 250-year history, from Benjamin Franklin’s mission to Paris during the Revolutionary War, to 21st-century challenges such as transnational terrorism, climate change and global health.

 

The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

 

Read more about the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training

Founded in 1986, ADST is a nonprofit, nonpartisan, 501(c)3 educational organization that has conducted and posted more than 2,500 transcripts of oral history interviews of former diplomats on its website — the world’s largest diplomatic oral history collection. ADST’s collection is a unique and priceless historical record of post-World War II U.S. diplomacy, praised by scholars, educators and diplomatic practitioners alike. ADST is committed to strengthening public appreciation of diplomacy’s contribution to America’s national interests, and enriching the professional knowledge of diplomatic practitioners.

 

- - - 

This event is a part of Diplomacy Week 2026! Diplomacy Week offers students and, on a couple occasions, members of the community, opportunities to engage closely with experts whose work has shaped U.S. foreign policy. Explore other events on the UNC Global Affairs website and join us in celebrating 250 years of American diplomacy!

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Plant Communities of North Carolina
location: North Carolina Botanical Garden, 100 Old Mason Farm Road, Chapel Hill, NC, 27517, United States
description:
Dates: Fridays, October 2, 9, 16, 2026 (3-sessions)
Time: 9:30 AM – 12:30 PM 
This 9-hour course introduces participants to the remarkable diversity of North Carolina’s native plant communities and the natural processes that shape them. Differences in geology, climate, soils, fire regimes, landscape position, and other environmental factors have given rise to an extraordinary variety of ecosystems. Through a combination of classroom instruction and outdoor exploration in the display gardens, participants will gain an understanding of the ecological and historical factors that have shaped the distribution, composition, and diversity of plant communities across the state.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Teen Science Café: Unwinding Spiral Galaxies
location: Downtown Raleigh, 11 West Jones Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
The winding arms of spiral galaxies are one of their most obvious features. By measuring how tightly the arms are wrapped, we can reveal clues about other components that are much harder to observe, such as dark matter content and central black hole mass. We aim to partner volunteers with AI in order to identify individual spiral arms in tens of thousands of galaxies, measure how tightly each arm is wound, and use those measurements to estimate these elusive properties. Doing so will help us better understand how galaxies similar to our own Milky Way form and evolve. 


About the Presenter
Dr. Patrick Treuthardt is the Assistant Head of the Astronomy & Astrophysics Research Lab at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences and a Research Affiliate in the Department of Computing Sciences at Coastal Carolina University. He studies the shapes, structures, and internal physics of nearby galaxies in order to better understand how they form and evolve. Dr. Treuthardt is the lead researcher of the Spiral Graph citizen science project and its follow-up, Cluster Buster.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Remembering in the Garden: Community Journaling in Nature

description:
In this community journaling in nature workshop, explore ways that gardens and stories can heal our minds and bodies. On a guided, meditative stroll amongst the grand and small sights, sounds and smells of Duke Gardens, you will be invited to notice, feel and remember. Dr. Zelda Lockhart, author, expressive arts therapist and Fulbright Specialist, will offer prompts to journal, draw and reconnect to each other and the natural ecology of the living and the dead. This workshop will offer activities that can be integrated as daily practice wherever you live and wherever you go, toward the goal of individual, ancestral and community healing. 
Presenter’s Bio: Dr. Zelda Lockhart is a current Fulbright Specialist who holds a PhD in Expressive Arts Therapies. Her novels, keynotes and workshops focus on the power of story and nature to connect us across boundaries constructed by colonialism and heal our generations from the wounds of colonialism. Visit her website at www.zeldalockhart.com.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage

description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Vintage Base Ball Day at the DAP
location: Historic Durham Athletic Park
description:
A day of vintage base ball played at the Historic Durham Athletic Park !

***Any tickets purchased for our 2025 Vintage Base Ball event are valid for 2026!***

The iconic Durham Athletic Park has hosted baseball games since 1926 and was even featured in an iconic baseball film, but Durham’s baseball roots are even deeper. The first century of baseball was marked by racial segregation and separate leagues for black and white athletes at the DAP until the 1950s; however, Duke Homestead welcomes all people to participate and honors the struggles and achievements of the many players over the past century who brought us the Durham baseball culture we know today. Players will wear historic uniforms, follow historic gameplay, and use historic equipment. The games will follow 1860 and 1869 Beadles Rules.

We invite you to connect with the history of this sport, this place, and this community by enjoying an afternoon out at the ball park.

Admission to the game is $10; children under 4 years old will be admitted free. Game tickets can be purchased online through Eventbrite, or in person at the Duke Homestead visitor center, as well as at the gate on game day. Early-Bird tickets for $5 available until 9/21 (online here or at the Duke Homestead visitor center).

Enjoy a family-friendly day at the ball park complete with “old fashioned” concessions, food, beer, and historic music. Spectators are encouraged to come dressed in your favorite historical, vintage, or retro inspired outfits. We believe in vintage style, not vintage values! Kids will get to play historic games with our costumed interpreters, as well as have the opportunity to run the bases in-between ball games.

Joining our local Duke Homestead team this year will be The Shiners from Rockingham, VA and a special team from the Durham Fire Department! The first game will be played at 11am, with games at 12:30pm and 2pm to follow.

This game is a fundraiser for the Duke Homestead State Historic Site and it is sponsored by the Duke Homestead Education and History Corporation (the site’s volunteer, non-profit support organization), Measurement, Inc., and Stone Brothers & Byrd.

Free parking available at the lot at 412 Morris St, Durham, NC 27701. A couple of handicap spaces are available in the DAP parking lot.

**We are unable to offer refunds on purchased tickets. All cancelled tickets will be considered a donation to the site and will be used for future educational programming.**

Apple Butter Making & 18th-Century Demonstrations: Take a walk through history and learn about the rich traditions of the past with live demonstrations of apple butter making and demonstrations like weaving, spinning, blacksmithing, and more!

Maker and Food Vendors: Explore a marketplace of creativity and flavor with local artisans showcasing their crafts and delectable treats. It's the perfect opportunity to discover unique treasures and savor delicious bites! Get ahead on your holiday shopping!

Live Music and Storytelling: Enjoy local and traditional Appalachian musicians and storytellers live and in-person! Mary Greene, Orville Hicks, Diandra Patterson, and more!

Hatchet Throwing (Paid Activity): Test your aim and have a blast with our hatchet-throwing activity. Suitable for ages 14+. It's a fun and exciting way for older kids to burn off energy and challenge their skills. And of course, it's just plain fun for adults!

Pumpkin Painting (Paid Activity): Unleash your inner artist and transform pumpkins into works of art at our painting station. A wonderful activity for all ages!

Kid's Costume Contest (Paid Activity): Dress to impress and participate in our costume contest! Prizes await the most creative and spooktacular outfits.

Pet Costume Contest (Paid Activity): Don't forget your furry friends! Show off their best costumes and compete for fantastic prizes in our pet costume contest.

Raffles: Enter our 50/50 raffle for a chance to win a cash prize. Who doesn't love that?!

And SO MUCH MORE Fall Goodness! Mark your calendar for a day filled with autumnal magic, laughter, and community spirit. The Appalachian Autumn Market & Fall Festival is an experience you won't want to miss!

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Introduction to Stata
description:
This course will cover two days (10/5/26 and 10/7/26). Attendance is required as the course will not be recorded.

This course introduces students to Stata and data management. It is tailored for non-users who want to learn how to manage data more effectively. Each day, the class will demonstrate how to use the commands, followed by hands-on exercises using sample datasets. By the end of the course, participants will be able to perform the following:• Use Stata’s Graphical User Interference (GUI) with dialog boxes
• Run Stata commands from the command window and from scripts (“do” files)
• Enter, transfer, and save data in different formats, e.g., Excel, SAS, SPSS, text files
• Inspect the contents of a Stata dataset
• Append, merge, and sort datasets
• Identify and clean duplicate records
• Calculate new variables
• Create and manage labels for variables and values
• Recode variables
• Work with blocks of observations (“by” processing)
• Perform row-wise calculations (groups of columns)
• Collapse data into summary tables
• Reshape between long and wide formats
• Save and reproduce your work with “do” files
• Obtain descriptive statistics
• Create graphs and tables
• Run basic statistical analyses, e.g., Ordinary Least Squares regression, correlation matrices, Chi-square tests, t-tests

Registration and fee (refundable for students) are required for Zoom link access.

title: AI Security Non-Neogtiables with Joyce Rancani
description:
On Oct. 5 at 1 p.m., join a virtual event with Joyce Rancani, chief technology security officer at Qualys, an industry-leading enterprise cyber risk and security platform.

 

In her presentation, “AI Security Non-Negotiables,” Rancani will discuss how as enterprise adoption accelerates from static chatbots to autonomous, action-taking AI agents, the attack surface expands into non-deterministic execution paths, prompt-driven exploitation and complex supply chain vulnerabilities.

 

Her session will break down the non-negotiables of securing autonomous systems across their entire lifecycle from the "brilliant basics" of zero trust identity and runtime blast-radius containment, to the rigorous principles of securely designing, building, deploying and continuously monitoring AI agents in production.

 

The event is free to join and does not require registration. Students seeking campus life experience (CLE) credit should RSVP for the event in Heel Life to receive credit.

 

This event is sponsored by the Information Security Office as part of National Cybersecurity Awareness Month.

title: Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design, Main Lobby
description:
Visit the Gregg Museum of Art & Design for the opening of the exhibition Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today and a keynote address by curator Jake Newsome, founder of The Pink Triangle Legacies Project. Newsome's keynote address, "Enemies of the State: The Nazi Persecution of LGBTQ+ People," will examine the complex motivations behind Nazi leaders' choice to persecute LGBTQ+ people and to present it as vital to the success of the Third Reich. A Q&A and a book signing will follow the presentation. Please register to attend.

Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today is a traveling exhibit that explores the persecution of queer and trans people under Nazi rule and the long, ongoing struggle to reclaim their histories. Beginning in Weimar Germany’s early LGBTQ+ movements, the exhibit traces how the Nazi regime targeted those deemed “undesirable” and how survivors faced continued criminalization and silence long after 1945. The exhibition will be on display at the Gregg Museum through Oct. 23.
source: NC State Gregg Museum of Art & Design

title: Ackland Film Forum: "Set It Off" (F. Gary Gray, 1996)
location: The Lumina Theater, 620 Market Street, Chapel Hill, 27516, United States
description:
Jada Pinkett Smith, Queen Latifah, and Vivica A. Fox anchor this energetic reworking of the heist film. After a series of setbacks leaves four Black women with few viable paths forward, they embark on a string of increasingly audacious bank robberies. Blending humor, suspense, and tragedy, Set It Off captures both the bonds of friendship and the pressures of race, gender, and economic inequality in 1990s urban America. 
This film will be introduced by Professor Daelena Tinnin-Gadson, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature. 
It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. 
UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event. 
  
About the Series: 
Join the Ackland Film Forum this fall for Socially Charged Crime Thrillers: Snapshots of Social Anxiety, a series that accompanies the Ackland exhibition Care and Concern: Recent Acquisitions of Modern and Contemporary Art. 
As vehicles of social commentary and stylistic bravura, crime thrillers often register the pressures and contradictions of their historical moment. Across nearly half a century, the films in this series stage encounters with political power, public trust, inequality, and ambition through assassination plots, botched robberies, and media-driven spectacle. 
From the crises of the late 1960s to the intensified media environments of the twenty-first century, these works show how genre cinema can capture social anxiety in real time. Each film stands both as a gripping narrative and as a record of a world under strain, where institutions falter and everyday life becomes fraught with conflict. 
The Ackland Film Forum is co-organized by the Ackland Art Museum and UNC Film Studies, housed in the UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature.
source: Ackland Art Museum, UNC Chapel Hill

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: AI for Research – Introduction to AI Tools in Qualitative Software
description:
This course is only open to the UNC Chapel Hill Community. You must have an active ONYEN to register. 

Please note: Registration is for INDIVIDUAL Attendee only so we can track capacity. Attendance is required as it will not be recorded.

AI for Research (AIR), a collaboration between the Odum Institute and the University Library: Driving Innovation Forward

Discover how artificial intelligence can streamline workflows, uncover hidden patterns, and empower breakthroughs in your field. Learn practical applications of AI through Odum Institute AIR series that can revolutionize your research process.

This course will introduce participants to generative AI tools in qualitative software—ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA, and NVivo. These tools can be used to summarize textual documents through AI-assisted memo writing and to support coding, with each program taking a different approach to integrating human judgment and AI features.

The course will also demonstrate how ChatGPT can be used to code textual data, how to create effective prompts, and how to import results from ChatGPT into qualitative software for further analysis. The course will be based on presentation and lecture but will provide brief exercises for hands-on exercises to be completed outside of the course.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

Theorizing Distributed Journalistic Authority Amid Newsfluencers, Algorithms, and Generative Systems

 

Who’s a Journalist in the Age of AI? addresses a critical development in the news media. In this talk, UNC-Chapel Hill’s Hussman School of Journalism and Media faculty member, Deb Aikat, PhD, will discuss how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reconfigures the epistemic boundaries of journalistic authority, credibility, and public verification in democratic discourse.

 

Dr. Aikat will discuss how AI is reshaping press freedom at a time when public trust in media has sunk to 28%, according to Gallup’s 2025 survey. He studies the shifting information landscape in the U.S. and India — the world’s oldest and largest democracies — tracing how digital platforms empower people to publish, protest, and participate in civic life beyond traditional newsrooms.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Introduction to Stata
description:
This course will cover two days (10/5/26 and 10/7/26). Attendance is required as the course will not be recorded.

This course introduces students to Stata and data management. It is tailored for non-users who want to learn how to manage data more effectively. Each day, the class will demonstrate how to use the commands, followed by hands-on exercises using sample datasets. By the end of the course, participants will be able to perform the following:• Use Stata’s Graphical User Interference (GUI) with dialog boxes
• Run Stata commands from the command window and from scripts (“do” files)
• Enter, transfer, and save data in different formats, e.g., Excel, SAS, SPSS, text files
• Inspect the contents of a Stata dataset
• Append, merge, and sort datasets
• Identify and clean duplicate records
• Calculate new variables
• Create and manage labels for variables and values
• Recode variables
• Work with blocks of observations (“by” processing)
• Perform row-wise calculations (groups of columns)
• Collapse data into summary tables
• Reshape between long and wide formats
• Save and reproduce your work with “do” files
• Obtain descriptive statistics
• Create graphs and tables
• Run basic statistical analyses, e.g., Ordinary Least Squares regression, correlation matrices, Chi-square tests, t-tests

Registration and fee (refundable for students) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Oct 7 - Building Composable Vision Workflows in FiftyOne
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
This workshop explores the [FiftyOne](https://docs.voxel51.com/index.html) plugin framework to build custom computer vision applications. You’ll learn to extend the FiftyOne App with Python based panels and server side operators, as well as integrate external tools for labeling, vector search, and model inference into your dataset views.

**Date, Time and Location**

Oct 7, 2026
9 AM - 10 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/building-composable-vision-workflows-in-fiftyone-october-7-2026)**

You’ll also automate repetitive tasks by writing custom workflows executing within the FiftyOne environment. Attendees will learn to transform FiftyOne from a visualization tool into a central hub for your vision stack.

What you'll learn:

* **Build Python plugins.** Define plugin manifests and directory structures to register custom functionality within the FiftyOne ecosystem.
* **Develop server side operators.** Write functions to execute model inference, data cleaning, or metadata updates from the App interface.
* **Build interactive panels.** Create custom UI dashboards using to visualize model metrics or specialized dataset distributions.
* **Manage operator execution contexts.** Pass data between the App front end and your backend to build dynamic user workflows.
* **Implement delegated execution.** Configure background workers to handle long running data processing tasks without blocking the user interface.
* **Build labeling integrations.** Streamline the flow of data between FiftyOne and annotation platforms through custom triggers and ingestion scripts.
* **Extend vector database support.** Program custom connectors for external vector stores to enable semantic search across large sample datasets.
* **Package and share plugins.** Distribute your extensions internally and externally
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
location: Presbyterian Heritage Center
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
location: Welborn Gallery
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
location: Kings Mountain Historical Museum
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Structural Equation Modeling (SEM)
description:
This short course will introduce you to the major ideas behind structural equation modeling (SEM) and equip you with the knowledge necessary to get started on your own analysis using this method. SEM is a valuable tool beyond traditional regression models due to its flexibility, as it allows researchers to test more complex relationships among variables and to account for measurement error in analysis.

This course will cover the basics of:
• Confirmatory factor analysis
• Path analysis
• Structural equation models with latent variables
• Evaluating indirect relationships between variables
• Using fit statistics to test competing hypotheses
Examples and exercises will use the R package lavaan, but content from this course will be directly applicable to other programs that estimate structural equation models, such as Mplus and Stata.

Participants should be familiar with regression modeling before taking this course. Experience using R will be helpful but is not required.

Registration and fee are required for Zoom link access.

title: Oct 8 - MCP, Agents and Skills Meetup Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on MCP, agents and skills.

**Date, Time and Location**

Oct 08, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/mcp-agents-skills-meetup-october-8-2026)**

**Designing Multi‑Agent Systems: Sequential, Parallel, and Beyond with ADK**

Multi‑agent systems are powerful but choosing the wrong interaction pattern can quickly lead to fragile, slow, or expensive AI systems.
In this talk, we explore the core multi‑agent design patterns enabled by ADK, including sequential, parallel, and more advanced coordination models. Rather than focusing on tools alone, we’ll look at how to think architecturally about agent collaboration.

You’ll learn:

* When sequential agents are the right choice and when they become a bottleneck
* How parallel agents improve speed and coverage (and the trade‑offs they introduce)
* Common failure modes in poorly designed agent interactions
* Practical criteria for choosing the right pattern based on task, latency, and reliability

By the end of the session, you’ll have a clear mental model for designing multi‑agent systems that are intentional, scalable, and production‑ready.

*About the Speaker*

[Dr Roushanak Rahmat](https://www.linkedin.com/in/roushanakrahmat/) is an Enterprise AI Architect, Google Developer Expert (AI & Cloud), and recognized among the Top 100 Women in Tech (2025). With a PhD in Artificial Intelligence and over 15 years of experience, she specializes in designing and delivering enterprise-scale Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Deep Learning solutions that transform industries including healthcare, finance, energy, and public services.

**Privacy by Deployment: Architecting Agent-Driven Localization Workflows for Regulated Environments**

Most enterprise AI today is private by promise - a DPA, a SOC 2 report, or a contract clause that says, "we won't train on your data". For a regulated buyer, these are remedies after a breach, not controls that prevent or contain one. For organizations in healthcare, finance, defense, and government, privacy often requires stronger guarantees: data residency, customer-controlled execution, and, in some cases, operation within air-gapped environments.

This session demonstrates how agentic AI can automate a localization workflow while operating within these constraints. Using a real-world localization pipeline as an example, we will show how agentic systems can coordinate translation, review, quality assurance, and content preparation tasks while incorporating human checkpoints for approval and oversight.

We will also walk through the architectural patterns that enable these workflows to run inside customer-controlled and air-gapped environments without transferring sensitive content outside the customer boundary. The session includes a live product demonstration.

Key Takeaways

* Architectural patterns for deploying agentic AI in air-gapped and customer-controlled environments
* How agentic systems can automate localization workflows while preserving critical human review and approval processes
* Practical considerations for operating agentic workflows in regulated environments with auditability and governance requirements

*About the Speaker*

[Shruti Joshi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/28shruti) is building an AI powered secure localization stack for regulated industries such as healthcare, legal, finance that cannot send their content to a typical hosted SaaS. She brings 12+ years of engineering and architecture experience to the question this talk addresses: how do you make an agentic AI system deployable inside a regulated perimeter.

**MCP Is the Interface; Skills Are the Operating Discipline**

This talk shows how MCP and Agent Skills work together in practical agent systems. MCP gives agents a standard interface to tools, data, and workflows; skills encode the operating discipline that makes those connections reliable. Using a sanitized field-operations ledger as the case study, the talk walks through source intake, normalized state, uncertainty labels, role prompts, QA gates, and share-safe status drafting.

*About the Speaker*

[Chuck Hernandez](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chuck-hernandez/) is an AI engineering and client-delivery leader with 10+ years across software, data platforms, and enterprise implementation, including 3+ years shipping production GenAI systems.

**Agentic engineering is about good guidance.**

Garbage Inn. Is garbage out? This is true. For many input and output processes. In biological life and in computer systems, and equally true when working with LLM’s. The better the prompt, the better the context, the better the focus, And the better the contextual awareness, the better the quality of the output the LLM’s generates.
This is the governance, art and practice of what we like to call agentic engineering, something I've been practicing over the last year.

*About the Speaker*

[Dimitri Geelen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dimitrigeelen/) builds things that don't need him once they're done. Frameworks, transitions, agentic systems — the measure of success is always the same: does it hold up when he leaves the room? He understands not just how to deploy, but what it takes for a new service to survive and scale inside a complex enterprise.

description:
Calling aspiring filmmakers, storytellers and creatives!

Carolina alumna Resita Heavenly Cox is an Emmy Award-winning film director, community organizer, educator and cultural philosopher whose practice centers on the concepts of Sun Ra’s myth-science.

This theoretical framework posits American Blackness as a myth, particularly within the confines of capitalism. Resita uses moving images to reinterpret the complexities of Black life through a “third cinema” and impact-focused documentary lens. Her filmmaking is a deeply personal, somatic practice that moves beyond conventional methods to prioritize community, care and collective well-being.

By holding a mirror up to audiences, her films craft a yet-to-be-conceived image of self. Resita’s work forces viewers to grapple with uncomfortable realities of the human condition, ultimately serving the goal of imagining and birthing a better way of being. She operates from the conviction that each individual spark is the foundation for revolutionary cultural change.

Resita is a Hulu/Kartemquin Accelerator Fellow, North Star Fellow, 2024 Rockwood Documentary Leaders Fellow (Ford Foundation), 2025 Chicken & Egg Eggcelerator Fellow and 2024-25 Grounded Possibilities Environmental Justice Fellow. She holds an MFA from Northwestern University and was named an Esteemed Artist by the City of Chicago in 2022.

title: Hanes Visiting Artist Lecture Series: Salvador Jiménez-Flores
location: Hamilton Hall, 100
description:
Department of Art and Art History

 

Salvador Jiménez-Flores (b. 1985, Jalisco, México) is an interdisciplinary artist whose work explores the politics of identity, double consciousness, colonization, migration, "the other," and futurism through socially conscious installation, public, and studio-based art. His practice spans community-based work, drawing, ceramics, prints, and mixed media sculpture.

 

Jiménez-Flores holds an MFA in Drawing from Kendall College of Art & Design (2014). He has received prestigious awards, including the 2021 United States Artist Fellowship, the Joan Mitchell Foundation Painters & Sculptors Grant, the New England Foundation for the Arts, and the Threewalls’ RaD Lab + Outside the Walls Fellowship. He has been commissioned for public sculptures, including The Richard Hunt Award, Artprize, and Grounds For Sculpture. His work has been exhibited in renowned institutions such as the National Museum of Mexican Art (Chicago, IL), Grand Rapids Art Museum (MI), Museum of Glass (Tacoma, WA), Bemis Center for Contemporary Arts (Omaha, NE), Grounds For Sculpture (Hamilton, NJ), Museum of Arts and Design (NYC), Crocker Art Museum (Sacramento, CA), and DePaul Art Museum (Chicago, IL), as well as The Print Center (Philadelphia, PA). Jiménez-Flores has served as Artist-In-Residence at institutions such as the City of Boston, Harvard Ceramics Program, Office of the Arts at Harvard University, Kohler Arts/Industry, Haystack Mountain School of Craft, Watershed Center for the Ceramic Arts, Museum of Glass, Chasen Thajni: El límite de lo propio in Puebla, México, Joan Mitchell Center in New Orleans, and Corning Museum of Glass. His work has been featured in prominent publications such as Ceramics Monthly, Newcityart, American Craft Magazine, Chicago Sun-Times, and others. His artwork is held in collections including the National Museum of Mexican Art, Grand Rapids Art Museum, Museum of Fine Arts, Kohler Company, and Museum of Glass.

 

Jiménez-Flores is currently an Associate Professor in Ceramics at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. He is a former organizer of The Color Network, which supports the advancement of people of color in ceramics, and is an organizing member of the Instituto Gráfico de Chicago, an activist art group inspired by Mexico’s Taller de Gráfica Popular.

 

An endowment established in 1983 through the generosity of Nancy and Robin Hanes supports the Art Department's Visiting Artist Series. This important program brings both established and emerging artists to campus to discuss their work in public lectures and to offer individual critiques to our M.F.A. students.  The Hanes Visiting Artist series greatly enriches both our academic programs and our outreach to the wider community.  All lectures are free and open to the public.
